title: Besieging Mahinda Rajapaksa,  Sri Lanka’s ethos, and SJB priorities | Daily FT
summary:

The ugliness of what’s happening now, in peacetime, cannot be hidden behind the façade of law. Some years ago, there were two fascinating legal re-enactments, one the trial of Socrates and the other, those of Jesus Christ. Both re-enactments concluded that given the laws at the time, the sentences were legally valid though phenomenally unjust. Slavery, segregation in Southern US, and apartheid in South Africa were legal in their time. Humanity and history put justice above unjust laws

‘The magistrate had permitted Shiranthi to visit her doctor at Nawaloka Hospital on Thursday, but the prison’s doctor said they wouldn’t be able to allow her to go to a private hospital…’

(https://www.examiner.media/shiranthi-denied-private-hospital-visit-namal-connected-to-indian-money-laundering-scam/)

Navi Pillay deserves the Nobel Prize for Peace because of the sincerity of her continuous, combative commitment to Human Rights, which made Nelson Mandela urge her to strive to be South Africa’s first non-white woman judge. She won the Nobel Prize because her juridical argumentation made the definitive case establishing Israel’s genocide against Gaza’s Palestinians. 

My applause is despite her strong critique of Sri Lanka during the decisive diplomatic battle at the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva in May 2009. She opened that Special Session with a forceful video address on a big screen to the Council from the UN in New York, calling for “an international investigation”. Speaking immediately after her, it was my task as Sri Lanka’s Ambassador/Permanent Representative to resolutely oppose her call and persuade the Council. We prevailed, 29 to12.  South Africa voted with us. 

Our relationship had no animosity. Before I left Geneva, Navi Pillay hosted my wife Sanja and me to a farewell lunch. Her parting pronouncement was: “Ambassador Jayatilleka, during your term here you performed a great service for your country, but a great disservice to the cause of human rights”.

The way we were

The Aristotelian term ‘ethos’ has come to mean the customary character, comprised of the constellation of morals, values, sentiments and guiding beliefs, of a community or collective entity.

The JVP took up arms unilaterally in 1971 and 1986. On neither occasion were its followers being killed by the State when it initiated warfare. 

The State defeated the JVP militarily. After each rebellion and a number of years in jail, the surviving JVP leaders were released by the State. 

JVP General Secretary Tilvin Silva who was incarcerated for participation in an armed attack on a high-value target, was among those released in 1994. 

No Asian State has been so flexible and forgiving against those imprisoned for organised civil war. Despite the extra-judicial execution of Rohana Wijeweera who was responsible for the murder of Vijaya Kumaratunga among thousands of others, his wife and children were safeguarded, housed and educated under State auspices, by Sri Lanka Navy. 

That was the bipartisan ethos of the Sri Lankan democratic State. 

TV images of the 73-year-old former First Lady, who never had the reputation of a Madam Marcos, and stayed by the side of her husband President Mahinda Rajapaksa throughout the war, not knowing when he would fall victim to an LTTE  assassin as did President Premadasa, Rajiv Gandhi and others, being bundled into a prison bus while wearing an eye patch after recent medical treatment in Singapore, demonstrates the huge difference between the ethos of the AKD-JVP-NPP dispensation and that of Sri Lanka’s State leadership since 1948. 

The ugliness of what’s happening now, in peacetime, cannot be hidden behind the façade of law. Some years ago, there were two fascinating legal re-enactments, one the trial of Socrates and the other, those of Jesus Christ. Both re-enactments concluded that given the laws at the time, the sentences were legally valid though phenomenally unjust. 

Slavery, segregation in Southern US, and apartheid in South Africa were legal in their time. Humanity and history put justice above unjust laws. 

In 1983/1984, my father Mervyn de Silva interviewed President JR Jayewardene, which involved an exchange on the Referendum of 1982 (reproduced in his magazine and newspaper columns). JRJ emphasised that the Referendum was “legal”. Mervyn responded with “But was it legitimate?”. The answer was silence. 

The law isn’t coterminous with either justice or legitimacy, both of which are held as higher values. 

A law which allows prolonged incarceration even when a person has not been convicted of any wrongdoing and may never be found guilty of one, is questionable from the standpoint of justice, fair-play and legitimacy. 

Moreover, the letter of the law must be observed without risking violence to the “spirit of the law”.  

A law, the spirit and logic of which aim to punish egregious fraud of public funds (such as the Central Bank bond scam), shouldn’t be deployed as ‘massive retaliation’ for misdemeanours which warrant a slap on the wrist and a fine. One doesn’t use a legal cannon to swat a fly of an offense. 

But then again, ‘overkill’, in its quite literal sense too, has been the JVP’s habit throughout its history. ‘Overkill’ proved the JVP’s undoing.

Code of Chivalry

On an island which holds four major world religions, there is a crosscutting, intermeshing, underlying sense of right and wrong, good and bad, that we are introduced to as children. This provides for a moral and ethical reflex that antedates knowledge of the letter of the law. It furnishes us with a basic sense of fairness and unfairness; indicates what one should be ashamed of and averse to. We develop a conscience. 

We absorb or form a code of conduct: what’s done and not done; what’s honourable and dishonourable. This ‘code’, probably introduced by parents, is reinforced or modified by what is taught in school and university, as well as our exposure to literature, theatre and cinema, and examples we encounter. 

The first book that the new State published in enormous numbers after the Cuban Revolution of January 1959 was a beautifully produced version of Don Quixote by Cervantes. This despite Karl Marx’s wry observation that the great novel revealed the impossibility of maintaining a noble, knightly code of chivalrous courage in an economy which was no longer medieval-feudal and had commenced transition to capitalism. 

The values of chivalry and courage to ‘tilt at windmills’ were components of the code of conduct of Fidel Castro and Che Guevara. Fidel kept insisting that “one must be chivalrous even when fighting the most wretched of enemies” and attributed his ‘code’ to his Spanish Jesuit teachers. In his last letter to his parents, Che mentioned that he ‘can feel once again the ribs of Rocinante’ between his heels—Rocinante being Don Quixote’s skinny old horse.

‘Chronicle of a Death Foretold’ 

A leadership with the slightest sense of honourable conduct; of things decent as opposed to mean-spirited and vicious, would know that a 73-year-old former wartime First Lady being taken from her home, and a few hours later, bundled into a prison bus, just doesn’t sit right; is downright ugly. There is a huge difference between decisive and ruthless; strict and wicked; sternly and sadistic. 

The Mafia had a code of not harming or taking hostage, wives, children and parents of rivals, but the Latin American drug cartels which came later don’t have such compunctions. The movie Scarface shows Al Pacino’s character Tony Montana, a Cuban deportee and gangster, angrily refusing to go through with the execution of the man designated for death by his Bolivian drug lord partner/patron, because the intended victim’s wife and kids had climbed into the car. Consequently, the cartel sends an armed band which executes Tony Montana by shot-gunning him in the back after he puts up a monumental gunfight. 

Under the AKD-JVP-NPP ‘power-cartel’, the State isn’t circumscribed in the matter of permissible targets, even by the parametric code of the movie’s anti-hero played by Pacino. No relative is off-limits, as seen in the collective treatment of the Rajapaksas, including a wife, mother, and grandmother/grand-aunt. 

AKD and his comrades  seem ignorant of ‘soft power’; of moral and ethical hegemony, of the moral high ground. You don’t intrinsically own the moral high ground. You occupy it or not according to how your discourse, conduct and character are widely perceived by universal norms. Even if you hold power, if you lose the moral high ground, you lose power—as Gotabaya Rajapaksa did. But if you don’t have power and yet occupy the moral high ground, you eventually win.  

AKD argues that all these persons are incarcerated because they are under investigation for various allegations of crimes according to existing laws. But proportionality is an indispensably crucial aspect of justice (as in Just War). Going by the Kalama Sutta, we must not rely on the authorities but ourselves inquire rationally whether the harsh treatment meted out to a septuagenarian former First Lady (and cardiac patient) is proportionate to the alleged offense. If not, we must question what really is going on. 

Under the AKD administration, the target menu of ‘lawfare’ constitutes two concentric circles.

The Rajapaksa family. 

The war-winning/wartime establishment extending from the Rajapaksas through ex-military top brass, to the State’s Tamil allies Douglas Devananda, Karuna Amman and Pillaiyan.

Connect the dots, and it seems punishment is being imposed for having won the war, defeated Prabhakaran. 

The object of all strategy being ‘the mind of the opposing commander’, it is deductively discernible who the ultimate target of all these exertions is: former president Mahinda Rajapaksa. Maverick MP Ramanathan Archchuna, medical doctor, speculatively raised in Parliament the likelihood that the legal witch-hunt against MR’s family and the shock of his wife jailed at Welikada could (intentionally) trigger a heart attack in Mahinda. 

Mahinda Rajapaksa is being besieged, his wife taken away, incarcerated, maltreated (denied her regular eye-specialist) so as to break his spirit and hasten his final exit. Already not in the best of health, sadness could weaken MR further and end him through emotional attrition—heartbreak. 

Does Mahinda really deserve what he is suffering emotionally and physically today, having liberated Sri Lanka from a thirty years war, reunified the island’s territory and restored peace and normalcy, not to mention vastly expanded the island’s infrastructure? 

Is this what his family members—whatever their mistakes and misdeeds—deserve for standing by him throughout the war years of extreme daily danger? A suicide-bomber, truck-bomb or the LTTE’s fledgling air-arm could have killed or crippled not only Mahinda but also his family.  

When making decisions that affect the lives of national personalities, especially aged ones, any fair, reasonable ruler or persons in authority should weigh such a person’s comparative merits and de-merits in the context of the larger role he/she played during one of the most extreme situations and existential crises of Lanka’s long, continuously chronicled history.   

Mahinda was there for his country, for us, when we needed him. He did what five previous leaders including four Presidents did not or could not do after the emergence of the threat of armed Tamil separatism. History and future generations will pose the question: where were his country and its citizens when he was besieged and mentally tormented in his old age? 

Will the psychological pressure and emotional torture that an old, visibly unsteady Mahinda Rajapaksa is being subjected to, be history’s record of the sense of gratitude of this State and nation? 

To my mother’s chagrin, my father never objected to me venturing independent opinions here and overseas even as a boy (Prof Kumari Jayawardena used to amusedly recall me still in school shorts, declaring my preference for Engels over Marx) or questioning my elders and betters at public seminars. However, Mervyn also imparted the importance of respect—for outstanding people who had contributed to their fields or the country (e.g., Shirley Amerasinghe, Gamini Corea, Godfrey Gunatilleke, Pieter Keuneman, N Sanmugathasan, GVS de Silva, Neville Kanakaratne, MDD Peiris, Bradman Weerakoon). 

AKD and colleagues have shown no respect, still less appreciation towards his outstanding predecessor Mahinda Rajapaksa whose achievement was historic, titanic.  

A Fulbright scholarship winner who abandoned his doctoral studies with Immanuel Wallerstein, Giovanni Arrighi, Mark Selden and James Petras in an irresistible compulsion to turn theory into praxis when JR Jayewardene conducted a coercive plebiscite instead of the scheduled General Election, I returned to a PhD in Brisbane twenty years later, after my parents died. The field being political philosophy, I was co-supervised, with my principal supervisor a profound political theorist, Emeritus Prof John Kane whose works are on Moral Capital, Virtue and Power, and Leadership. My co-supervisor from philosophy, Jeffrey Minson, authored a book on Nietzsche and Foucault. 

Jeff Minson’s studies led him to identify a crucial determinant which he specialised in over the next years: what the French call civilité, the quality of civility. Civilité is undermined by what Nietzsche denounced as ressentiment (resentment). 

Resentment has always been the animating drive of the JVP. Barbarically murderous towards (handsome, charismatic) Vijaya Kumaratunga, what form does/will it take towards Namal Rajapaksa?

‘History Will Absolve Me!’ was Fidel Castro’s legendary defence speech after the defeat of the 1953 Moncada uprising . History has absolved Mahinda Rajapaksa and rendered him immortal in the nation’s history and collective consciousness. Will History absolve AKD and the JVP-NPP for their callous, cruel treatment of Mahinda Rajapaksa, the patriarch of patriotism? 

Today’s legal ‘Great Terror’, non-lethal ‘legal guillotine’ and AKD’s angry, bitter rhetoric, recall Robespierre, whose weaponisation of ‘radical virtue’ and rampant guillotining of the old elite and moderate dissenters triggered such a backlash that he met the identical fate in a few years—the rollback ultimately enthroning ‘a man on horseback’, military hero Napoleon Bonaparte. 

In a preponderantly Buddhist country, compassion is an esteemed value, not least in a ruler. What will be the sociopolitical ‘karmic’ consequence in this lifetime, of AKD’s absence of compassion? 

Mao Zedong pronounced that not every death is of equal weight. Some are ‘as light as a feather’, while others are ‘as heavy as Mount Tai’. The death of a beloved hero who has served the people and the nation, is tragic and weighs like a mountain on the collective hearts of the people. When Mahinda dies, his death will weigh on the hearts of the people and nation as heavily as a mountain. By contrast, the downfall of “rulers and authorities”, and “wickedness in high places” (St Paul to the Ephesians, 6:12) may prove feather-light.

SJB’s situation 

As Dilum Alagiyawanna’s Daily FT piece reveals, from 2020 to 2025, the SJB as party secured 23.90%, 17.66%, and 21.69% respectively. (https://www.ft.lk/columns/Beyond-coalition-arithmetic-Rethinking-Opposition-strategy-after-Aragalaya/4-798481)

That’s: 

An average of 21.08% 

A drop from 2020. 

Stagnation in the 20% silo of the undivided UNP at the Feb 2018 Local Government election. 

20%+ is the maximum ‘market share’ of UNP-SJB ideology. 

The SJB’s self-imprisonment in the Ranil-UNP economic paradigm caused Sajith to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory in 2024, installing AKD-JVP rule and all its consequences.  

Sajith’s loss by 10% each time (2019, 2024) results from the drag effect of his party’s ideology. 

Sajith’s performance always betters his party due to a proto-populist ‘legacy’ element. 

Sajith must mainstream his social-democratic ideology, in his party. 

The SJB’s slew of victories at the Cooperative Society elections through ‘tactical voting’ and consensual leadership of a grassroots Opposition bloc is a viable strategic model.  

Constructing counter-power in the public arena to countervail Government dominance in Parliament (as JR-Premadasa did through Satyagraha); battling for democratic space against the JVP-NPP’s authoritarian measures  today, thereby enabling free elections in 2029, is the priority.

Never in history has a one-party dictatorship or threat of one, been defeated by one party/entity alone; only by a concert of diverse powers (WWII) or resistance movement of political parties and civic organisations.

title: From stability to prosperity: Building on President’s agenda | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 00:13
-     - 15

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

A small, empowered project-delivery unit reporting to the Cabinet, with authority to resolve inter-agency issues for projects of national importance, would cut timelines dramatically. Pairing it with clear performance indicators for agency heads, linked to approval times and project completion, would embed a culture of delivery across the public service. The Government’s strong focus on efficiency and integrity gives it a natural mandate to lead this change which could be a defining factor of competitive edge

The President’s discussion at Sri Lanka Economic Summit 2026 set out a confident, investment-friendly direction. With a few additions, it can become the blueprint for Sri Lanka’s next growth chapter.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s discussion at Fireside Chat at the Sri Lanka Economic & Investment Summit 2026 on 12 October sent a clear and welcome message: Sri Lanka is open for private investment, and the Government means business.

The announcements were substantive. Private operating rights for the East Container Terminal. A USD1.4 billion breakwater to unlock West Container Terminal phase II. A fresh tender for a logistics centre inside Colombo Port and a PPP container examination yard at Kerawalapitiya. Relief on the bunkering industry from SSCL and private investment in bunker storage, known as JCT Oil Bank. Four power transmission lines, as part of national power grid to be tendered to private investors, a Singapore-supported AI skills centre and tax relief for rural investment.

Taken together, they mark a pragmatic shift towards partnership with the private sector. This article builds on that direction and suggests complementary steps that can turn a strong agenda into a sustained growth story.

A strong foundation to build on

The Government deserves credit for what has already been achieved. Reserves are being rebuilt, credit ratings have improved and the country is on track to meet its IMF program targets. The President’s insistence that growth must protect these gains reflects sound economic judgement.

The energy record is equally encouraging. About 1,500 MW of solar has been added since the Government took office, with another 1,100 MW contracted. Renewables now supply around 69% of generation, and the country has gone days without diesel-fired power. The move from fixed feed-in tariffs to competitive tenders will lower costs for households and industry alike.

The President also opened the door to a growth-oriented successor arrangement with the IMF. That is the right instinct. Stabilisation has served its part; the natural next step is a deliberate transition to investment-led growth.

The President’s address showed a Government that is confident, pragmatic and ready to partner with the private sector. That is a strong platform.

A pragmatic framework for the growth phase

To move from stability to sustained growth of 5–6% a year, the summit’s announcements can be anchored in a simple, practical framework:

1.Integrate with global supply chains by targeting the sectors Sri Lanka can win.

2.Accelerate strategic infrastructure through private capital.

3.Enact the PPP law to give that capital a secure foundation and attract capital investment through right structure.

4.Build a best-in-region business environment, measured against our competing neighbours.

5.Modernise agriculture using AI and digital tools.

6.Reform the labour market for a productive, inclusive workforce.

Each pillar extends what the Government has already begun. The sections below take them in turn.

1. Joining global supply chains

The port reforms give Sri Lanka a powerful head start. A more efficient Colombo hub, with ECT under an experienced operator and WCT II adding capacity in the future would undoubtedly place Sri Lanka at a greater advantage and lowers logistics costs for exporters.

The next step is to pair this hub with a clear sector strategy. Manufacturers are diversifying their supply chains across Asia, and Sri Lanka’s location on the East–West shipping lane is a natural advantage. A short list of priority sectors, such as electronics assembly, higher-value apparel, processed food, pharmaceuticals, marine services and digital services, each with a dedicated investment package of land, incentives and skills, would turn port capacity into export growth.

2. Strategic infrastructure for a growth push

The port and electricity transmission grid projects show the Government’s appetite for transformative infrastructure. Two further projects would amplify that momentum:

Projects on this scale, alongside storage, transmission and urban transport, call for capital beyond the public budget. The president’s remark emphasising on PPPs shows that Government recognise it as a priority, however, the missing piece is the legal framework.

3. The PPP law: the keystone of the agenda

Nearly every project the President announced, from ECT and Kerawalapitiya to floating solar at Randenigala and new transmission lines, is envisaged as a public-private partnership. A dedicated PPP Act would give all of them a common, secure foundation.

Sri Lanka has used PPPs since the 1990s, and a PPP law has been discussed for nearly two decades. This Government has brought it closer than ever: a draft Bill was published for public comment in 2025, with technical support from the Asian Development Bank, and officials have signalled their intent to introduce it soon.

Enacting it would provide:

Passing the PPP Act, with the refinements proposed by the Ceylon Chamber and other stakeholders, would be the single most powerful way to deliver the President’s pledge of predictable rules and stronger investor protection. Budget 2027 offers the ideal moment to set a firm date.

4. A best-in-region business environment

The President’s pledge of transparency, investor protection and infrastructure support sets the right narrative. The opportunity now is to make Sri Lanka not merely competitive with its competing peers, but the easiest place in South Asia to start, run and grow a global business.

Investors compare destinations on practical questions. How quickly can a company be registered? How long does it take to secure land, a building permit or a power connection? How fast does cargo clear? How reliably are contracts enforced? Sri Lanka can set itself an ambition to match or beat the best in the region, including Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand, on every one of these measures.

A practical reform package could include:

The most valuable reform may also be the least costly: better coordination across inter-governmental agencies. A single project can need approvals from the BOI, UDA, Central Environmental Authority, local and provincial authorities, line ministries and the Treasury.

A small, empowered project-delivery unit reporting to the Cabinet, with authority to resolve inter-agency issues for projects of national importance, would cut timelines dramatically. Pairing it with clear performance indicators for agency heads, linked to approval times and project completion, would embed a culture of delivery across the public service. The Government’s strong focus on efficiency and integrity gives it a natural mandate to lead this change which could be a defining factor of competitive edge.

5. An AI-driven agricultural revolution

The President’s attention to rural investment opens the door to one of Sri Lanka’s biggest opportunities. Agriculture still employs a large share of the workforce, nearly 23%, yet its productivity lags well behind the rest of the economy. Global advances in artificial intelligence and digital farming can close that gap faster than ever before.

Around the world, farmers are using AI to decide what to plant, when to irrigate and how much fertiliser to apply. Satellite and drone imagery detect crop stress and disease early. Mobile advisory services deliver tailored guidance in local languages. Digital marketplaces connect smallholders directly with buyers and exporters.

Sri Lanka can adopt these tools at scale:

Paired with the new AI skills centre, these steps could turn agriculture from a source of rural vulnerability into an export engine and a driver of rural prosperity.

6. A modern, inclusive labour market

Skilled labour force is the biggest asset in Sri Lanka. Modernising labour laws would enable more conducive environment and will cater for the changing global economy.

Existing labour laws, including laws such as the Shop and Office Employees Act of 1954 and the Termination of Employment of Workmen Act of 1971, was designed for a very different economy. Consolidating labour laws into a single, modern code would bring clarity for workers and employers alike.

Priorities could include:

Reforms designed through dialogue with employers and trade unions would balance fairness with flexibility, and give investors confidence that Sri Lanka’s workforce is ready to grow with them.

The IMF program offered the country a firm footing, long awaited macro stability. With right plans, Sri Lanka can rollout a growth strategy within next two years. Budget 2027 is the ideal place to begin, and the private sector stands ready to play its part

A moment of opportunity

The President’s address showed a Government that is confident, pragmatic and ready to partner with the private sector. That is a strong platform.

With a clear growth framework, deeper integration into global supply chains, strategic infrastructure, an enacted PPP law, a best-in-region business environment, AI-powered agriculture and a modern labour market, Sri Lanka can turn the stability it had earned into lasting prosperity.

The IMF program offered the country a firm footing, long awaited macro stability. With right plans, Sri Lanka can rollout a growth strategy within next two years. Budget 2027 is the ideal place to begin, and the private sector stands ready to play its part.

(The writer is a CFA charterholder and holds the FRM designation, with prior experience at the Central Bank of Sri Lanka and the Ministry of Finance. title: Corruption: Promises and Results | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 00:08
-     - 10

Sri Lanka should not have a system in which corruption becomes a political weapon used against opponents while the same standards are not applied to one’s own political allies. Nor should the country depend on the personal courage of one politician, one investigator or one judge

Sri Lankans have heard these promises many times: corruption will be defeated, those responsible will be brought before the courts, and money taken from the public will be recovered and many more.

It is these promise that resonates strongly, particularly in the minds of the ordinary people. After all, when public money is lost, it is ultimately the public that carries the burden through higher taxes, higher prices, reduced services and increased Government debt.

The present Government came to power on the solemn promise, prior to the General Election in 2024 among other things, investigating complaints within six months, establishing special arrangements for financial-crime cases, revisiting cases previously withdrawn by the Bribery Commission and the Attorney General, and establishing an independent Directorate of Public Prosecution, these are ambitious commitments. Governing a country is very different from making promises prior to a General Election.

The Governing party was aware that they were inheriting institutions with considerable weaknesses. Investigations can take years. Financial transactions can cross borders. Evidence has to meet the requirements of a criminal court. Prosecutors have to establish individual responsibility rather than simply demonstrating that a Government project or policy resulted in a loss.

There is therefore a legitimate argument that some cases cannot be resolved quickly. But that explanation cannot become an excuse for endless delay. The question ordinary citizens ask is simple: What has been actually achieved?

An investigation and or arrest is not a conviction. A court case is not recovery of public money.  A press conference announcing action against corruption does not, by itself, put a single rupee back into the Treasury. This is particularly important when very large sums of public money is involved.

Sri Lanka’s highest Court has already made an important distinction. In its 2023 judgment concerning the economic crisis, the Court found that several senior officials, including former Presidents and a former Finance Minister had breached the public trust in their management of the country’s economy. That was a significant judicial finding, but it was not a criminal conviction that those individuals personally stole a particular amount of money.

This distinction matters because Sri Lanka must not replace one injustice with another. People accused of corruption are entitled to due process, just as ordinary citizens are. At the same time, the public is entitled to expect serious allegations involving public money to be investigated thoroughly and without unnecessary delay.

Uncomfortable issue

There is another uncomfortable issue.

The longer a case takes, the more difficult it can become to establish what happened. Documents disappear, memories fade, witnesses become unavailable and financial assets can move between jurisdictions. This is why an effective anti-corruption system must be designed to act expeditiously, independently and professionally.

The Government has taken some steps in this direction. Parliament approved the referral of several COPA and COPE findings to the Attorney General and CIABOC in July 2026. The Government has also introduced reforms relating to asset declaration and beneficial ownership, while CIABOC has launched an electronic asset-declaration system. 

The IMF has noted these reforms as part of Sri Lanka’s broader governance. These developments should be acknowledged.

But there is also evidence of continuing difficulties. In September 2026, CIABOC’s Director General publicly questioned whether some of the NPP’s manifesto commitments could be implemented because of existing legal and institutional constraints.

This raises an important question: Were the difficulties underestimated when those promises were made? Perhaps they were. The reforms of the Govt. machinery are more complicated than many people surmised. But if that is the case, the Government should explain this honestly to the public.

Citizens understand that institutional reforms take time. What is much harder for them to accept is hearing promises of swift action and then watching important cases continue for years without seeing convictions or significant recovery of public assets.

This is not an argument against the present Government. It is an argument for accountability regardless of who is in power.

Sri Lanka should not have a system in which corruption becomes a political weapon used against opponents while the same standards are not applied to one’s own political allies. Nor should the country depend on the personal courage of one politician, one investigator or one judge.

We need institutions strong enough to withstand political pressure. We need professional investigators who can follow the money. We need prosecutors who can act independently. We need courts capable of dealing with complex financial cases without delay. The Govt. should make available to the Prosecutors and the Courts all resources and facilities on time to reduce the time taken to conclude cases. 

We need mechanisms capable of freezing and recovering assets when the law permits it, including assets transferred overseas. And above all, we need transparency.

The public should be able to see, case by case, what was alleged, what was investigated, what evidence was found, what happened in the courts and perhaps most importantly how much public money was actually recovered. The last figure deserves far more attention than the number of arrests.

The poor citizens do not benefit merely because somebody is arrested. The taxpayer does not recover money merely because a case is filed. Justice is not complete simply because a politician is questioned by an investigating agency. The ultimate test is whether the law establishes the truth, holds people accountable where wrong doing is proved, and returns the unlawfully obtained public assets to the people.

Sri Lanka has already paid an enormous price for weak governance. We should therefore demand something more lasting than another promise to fight corruption.

We need a system in which no Government can easily protect the powerful, and in which public money is treated as exactly what it is: the people’s money.

title: When hospital measurements go wrong, patient safety is at stake! | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 00:05
-     - 11

A leading private hospital has raised serious concerns about the accuracy of its patient measurements.

Last week, when my wife visited the hospital for a DEXA scan, a nurse recorded her weight and height before the procedure. Subsequently, when we cross-checked these measurements at a clinic where she regularly attends medical check-ups, we discovered a staggering discrepancy: her weight had been overstated by 10kg, while her height had been understated by 7cm.

Was the weighing scale defective, or was this the result of human error or negligence? Whatever the explanation, such discrepancies warrant an immediate investigation. Accurate height and weight measurements are important clinical data, and errors can potentially affect medical assessments, dosage calculations where weight is relevant, and treatment decisions.

I therefore request the relevant authorities, including the Sri Lanka Standards Institution (SLSI) and the appropriate health-sector regulatory bodies, to ensure that weighing scales and other measuring equipment used in hospitals are regularly inspected, calibrated and maintained, with staff properly trained to record measurements accurately.

I also appeal to the Health Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa, to look into this matter and consider appropriate measures to safeguard patients from preventable errors. Private hospitals that charge substantial fees must be accountable for the accuracy, quality and reliability of the services they provide.

Patient safety must never be compromised by faulty equipment or inaccurate record-keeping.

Mohamed Zahran, Colombo

title: Sri Lanka swamp Bangladesh in dress rehearsal game | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 03:39
-     - 3

Sri Lanka thumped Bangladesh by eight wickets after bowling them out for 58 in the final league match of the Pakistan Women’s Under19 T20 Tri-Series played at Iqbal Stadium, Faisalabad yesterday.

It was Sri Lanka’s fifth win on the trot and their third in as many matches against Bangladesh in the Tri-Series.

The match was a dress rehearsal for Sunday’s final where the two teams will meet each other once again.

Bangladesh batters were all at sea against the right-arm medium-paced deliveries of Danodya Sewmini (2/7) and right-arm leg-spin of Limansa Thilakarathna (3/13) as they collapsed inside 18 overs. Only Mymuna Nahar (23) and Sadia Akter (17) got into double figures.

Sri Lanka knocked the runs off in the 11th over losing two wickets. Vimoksha Balasuriya scored 22 off 18 balls at the top. The win was completed by Nethmi Upeksha (17*) and Limansa (10*) who was named Player of the Match.

Scores: 

Bangladesh Women 58 (17.3) (Mymuna Naher 23, Sadia Akter 17, Danodya Sewmini 2/7, Limansa Thilakarathna 3/13) lose to Sri Lanka Women 59-2 (10.4) (Vimoksha Balasuriya 22, Nethmi Upeksha 17*)

History was made as the Jaffna Bulls etched their name into Sri Lankan sports folklore, being crowned champions of the very first Next XV rugby tournament following a sensational, high-intensity performance in the Grand Final.

The championship victory marks the culmination of a groundbreaking campaign for the Bulls, whose pioneering approach, combining AI-driven draft selections, drone training analysis, and high-performance athlete care, translated into ultimate glory on the pitch.

The final clash against the Galle Lions, who were on an unbeaten streak, lived up to the occasion, featuring pace, discipline, and dramatic shifts in momentum.

From the opening whistle, the Bulls established dominance through their forward pack, standing strong in defence and then delivering clinical set-piece execution at the scrum and lineout. The tactical preparation paid off early as the Bulls controlled territory and broke through the defense with sharp, quick-phase play out wide.

The Bulls took charge early through patient build-up play and sharp game management from their leaders, pinning the opposition in their own half and converting pressure into crucial scoreboard points. In the closing minutes, the Bulls’ physical conditioning proved to be the differentiator. The team displayed remarkable composure under pressure, securing key turnovers and controlling the clock to seal a historic victory as the final whistle blew.

Reflecting on the victory, Jaffna Bulls Co-owner Dhovika Senevirathne paid tribute to the relentless dedication across all levels of the organisation:

“To be crowned the very first champion of the Next XV tournament is an incredible feeling, but more than anything, it is a validation of the effort put in behind the scenes. From our coaches to our recovery staff, management, and sponsors, everyone worked tirelessly with a single vision. Most of all, the boys gave everything on the field. They trusted the process, bought into our culture from day one, and delivered when it mattered most.”

Beyond the trophy, the victory highlights the transformative impact of the Next XV tournament on youth rugby in Sri Lanka. Designed as a bridge between school-leaver rugby and high-performance environments, the tournament gave emerging talent a stage to test themselves at a higher level.

Crucially, the Bulls succeeded in taking players from traditional school rivalries across the island and forging them into a tight-knit family:

“This tournament is so important for the future of Sri Lankan rugby and for these young players,” added Co-owner Prad Navaratnam. “In Sri Lanka, school rugby rivalries are fierce and deeply rooted. But one of the proudest achievements of this season was watching boys from different rival schools come together under the Jaffna Bulls banner. They set those long-standing rivalries aside, backed each other like brothers, and played as one united team. That is what sport is truly about, and that unity is why we are champions today.”

With the inaugural trophy secured, the Jaffna Bulls have established a new benchmark for franchise rugby in Sri Lanka, proving that data-led preparation, professional standards, and strong team culture are a winning formula.

title: Iconic Kithulgala Rest House begins a new chapter as EKHO Kithulgala | Daily FT
summary:

The iconic Kithulgala Rest House, a much-loved landmark in Sri Lanka’s hospitality history, has been reimagined as EKHO Kithulgala, becoming the seventh property under the growing EKHO Hotels & Resorts portfolio. The transformation marks a new chapter for this historic riverside retreat, preserving its nostalgic charm and heritage while introducing refreshed accommodation and improved facilities for the modern traveller.

For generations, the Kithulgala Rest House has been a familiar destination for travellers journeying through Sri Lanka’s lush wet zone. Whether as a scenic stopover, a peaceful riverside escape or a base for exploring the surrounding wilderness, the property has created lasting memories for countless visitors. Its transition to EKHO Kithulgala seeks to carry this legacy forward, retaining the character and sense of familiarity that have long defined the rest house experience.

The property now features 20 refreshed guest rooms, comprising of Garden View and River View accommodation, complemented by improvements to its public spaces. While enhancing guest comfort, the transformation has been approached with sensitivity towards the property’s heritage, ensuring that the essence of the former rest house remains an integral part of the EKHO Kithulgala experience.

Situated along the banks of the Kelani River, EKHO Kithulgala occupies a remarkable location surrounded by tropical rainforest and rich biodiversity. For decades, the former Kithulgala Rest House has welcomed birdwatchers, naturalists and wildlife enthusiasts, establishing itself as a familiar base for those exploring the region’s exceptional birdlife.

This longstanding association continues as EKHO Kithulgala positions itself as an ideal base camp for birdwatching and nature exploration. With easy access to the Makandawa Forest Reserve, a renowned habitat for endemic and resident bird species, guests can venture into the surrounding rainforest for early morning birdwatching excursions, guided nature walks and immersive wildlife experiences.

Beyond birdwatching, Kithulgala is widely recognised as one of Sri Lanka’s premier destinations for white-water rafting. EKHO Kithulgala enjoys a particularly distinctive advantage, with the rafting route ending directly at the property, allowing adventure enthusiasts to conclude their river experience at the doorstep of their accommodation.

The destination also holds a special place in cinematic history through its association with the Academy Award-winning film  'The Bridge on the River Kwai,' filmed in the Kithulgala area during the 1950s, adding another fascinating dimension to the region’s heritage.

The opening of EKHO Kithulgala follows the recent transformation of the former Belihuloya Rest House into EKHO Belihuloya, further strengthening the brand’s presence in Sri Lanka’s nature and adventure tourism landscape.

Together, these properties reflect a broader commitment to revitalising Sri Lanka’s iconic rest houses, preserving their historical significance while introducing contemporary comforts and destination-led experiences.

More than a change of name, EKHO Kithulgala represents the continuation of a cherished legacy. It is a place where generations of memories remain part of the experience, where nature and adventure are never far away, and where the spirit of the iconic Kithulgala Rest House lives on.
